name: Tanco Mine (Bernic Lake)
description: Canada's only producing lithium mine and one of the world's largest cesium sources. Operating since 1969; Sinomine bought it in June 2019 for $135M and restarted spodumene production in late 2021. Throughput about 400 t/day.
regulatory_notes: Original licence No. 973 dates from 1983. A cesium plant amendment was filed in 2022 and a 2023 Notice of Alteration allowed milling of ore from other properties. A new comprehensive licence replaced the 1983 one and excluded the proposal to partly drain Bernic Lake. Appeals against the new licence were dismissed by cabinet order — the Wilderness Committee objected not to the licence but to the appeal route, since the only recourse is to the same minister whose department issued it. In 2022 Ottawa ordered three other Chinese firms to divest Canadian lithium assets; Sinomine kept Tanco.

name: Falcon West cesium project
operator_raw: Grid Metals (85%) / Avenir Minerals, an Agnico Eagle subsidiary (15%)
co_owners: Avenir Minerals, an Agnico Eagle subsidiary (15%)
description: Drilled October 2025 to March 2026. About 50,000 t of rock containing roughly 1,300 t of cesium — described by the company as the second-largest cesium deposit to be developed in the Western world, and roughly half of one year's global supply. Small enough that it might be mined out in a year. 130 km east of Winnipeg, 500 m north of the Trans-Canada.
regulatory_notes: An Environment Act licence filing is planned by the end of 2026. Consent from Sagkeeng First Nation has not been given and talks are ongoing; Chief E.J. Fontaine describes the relationship positively and two members have worked as technicians on the prospecting team, while saying environmental concerns and economic benefits still have to be worked out. Note the word used is consent, not consultation. Added from Winnipeg Free Press reporting — this entry did not appear in the underlying research and is the least checked here.

name: Tanco open pit / Bernic Lake drainage concept
description: A 2023 proposal to partly drain Bernic Lake for open-pit access.
regulatory_notes: Explicitly excluded from the replacement licence. Would almost certainly trigger federal permits.

name: Tanco concentrator and cesium plant expansion
commodity: Lithium and cesium concentrates; cesium nitrate and carbonate
description: A CAD 176M, 1 Mtpa processing plant approved in February 2023.
regulatory_notes: Cesium plant expansion filed as an Environment Act Proposal amendment in 2022.

name: Donner Lake lithium

name: Thompson Mine Complex
operator_raw: Vale Base Metals, transferring to Exiro / Orion / Canada Growth Fund consortium (81.1%)
co_owners: transferring to Exiro / Orion / Canada Growth Fund consortium (81.1%)
description: Two underground mines and a mill on the 135 km Thompson Nickel Belt. In February 2026 Vale agreed to transfer majority ownership to a consortium including the federal Canada Growth Fund, with up to US$200M committed.
regulatory_notes: Operates under long-standing provincial licences; no Commission referral was found for the change of control. Vale's Q2 2026 statements still describe Thompson as held for sale, so closing is not confirmed. Nickel, copper and cobalt are all on Canada's critical minerals list.

name: Birchtree Mine
description: Underground mine southwest of Thompson.

name: Pipe Lake deposit
description: Historic Thompson Nickel Belt deposit.

name: Thompson smelter and refinery
description: Former integrated smelter and refinery. Closure dates unverified.

name: Minago Critical Minerals Project
commodity: Nickel, platinum group metals, magnesium, aggregate
operator_raw: Norway House Cree Nation (Minago Development GP)
description: Wholly owned by Norway House Cree Nation since November 2024, bought from Flying Nickel for about $8M plus share surrender. Resource of roughly 690–722 Mlb nickel measured and indicated, plus palladium and platinum. The first phase quarries dolomite for low-emission magnesium before nickel — the community describes this as using the entire animal.
regulatory_notes: Environment Act Licence No. 2981 issued August 2011 to Victory Nickel for a 10,000 t/day open pit. Changes proposed in 2022 triggered consultation with Norway House, Misipawistik, Mosakahiken, Pimicikamak and the Manitoba Métis Federation. The amended licence was announced in March 2026. No Commission hearing was held. Manitoba committed $2M toward the magnesium phase at PDAC 2026. The site lies inside the Norway House Resource Management Area — the one RMA overlap verified in the research. Marketed by the community as removing the usual consultation hurdle through direct ownership.

name: Lalor Mine
description: Anchor of the Snow Lake operations. In September 2026 Hudbay extended reserve life to 2043, with reserves of 27 Mt containing 2.0 Moz gold and production averaging about 185,000 oz/yr.
regulatory_notes: No Commission history found. Zinc concentrate moves by rail to Churchill for export to Europe, 2026 being the third consecutive year.

name: Stall Concentrator

name: New Britannia Mill

name: Britannia gold project

name: 777 Mine

name: Flin Flon metallurgical complex
description: Concentrator on care and maintenance. Hudbay is studying flow-sheet changes to reprocess the tailings for critical minerals and precious metals.
regulatory_notes: Wildfires forced a regional evacuation in May 2025.

name: Thompson Brothers lithium deposit
description: Spodumene pegmatite on the Grass River linking Wekusko Lake with Crowduck Bay. Resource figures conflict badly across sources — roughly 8–11 Mt at about 1% Li₂O from company-linked sources; one trade site's 73.6 Mt figure is inconsistent with everything else and should not be used.
regulatory_notes: No Environment Act filing found. The company has renamed repeatedly and pivoted toward uranium elsewhere, so the Manitoba lithium project appears deprioritised.

name: Grass River lithium deposit
description: Second deposit of the Snow Lake lithium project.

name: CentrePort lithium hydroxide plant
operator_raw: Snow Lake Resources / LG Energy Solution
description: Proposed battery materials plant.

name: Gordon deposit (former Farley Lake mine)
description: The higher-grade pit, to be mined first.
regulatory_notes: Federal assessment completed March 2023 with a positive decision statement. Separate provincial licence issued.

name: MacLellan deposit and mill
description: 9,000 t/day mill. About 186,000 oz/yr over a 25-year life, roughly 3 Moz total. Initial capital raised to $937M. First production expected in the first half of 2029, delayed from 2028 by the 2025 wildfire evacuation.
regulatory_notes: Environment Act Licence No. 3391, with a Notice of Alteration approved 26 March 2026. The only Manitoba mineral project in this catalogue to go through a full federal environmental assessment, completed March 2023. Benefit agreements are in place with both proximate First Nations: Marcel Colomb signed in June 2023, Mathias Colomb in 2025 while its judicial review of the federal decision statement was being resolved. No provincial Commission hearing.

name: Lynn Lake legacy mine
description: Farley headframe and mill demolished; tailings cover options under review.
regulatory_notes: One of five priority orphaned and abandoned mine sites under a $50.7M five-year commitment.

name: Ruttan Mine
description: More than 1.3 million cubic metres of clay placed over the tailings.

name: Sherridon / Camp Lake
description: The Sherritt-Gordon mine operated 1931–51 and left about 7 Mt of acid-generating tailings over 47 hectares. Remediation began in 2009 and construction was declared complete in 2022.
regulatory_notes: The province considers this finished; the Manitoba Métis Federation does not. It says many Red River Métis citizens still have concerns, and earlier reporting documented local distrust. Manitoba created a Sherridon Collaboration Table in March 2024. A good test case for whether a closed file is actually closed.

name: Eden Lake carbonatite
description: Manitoba's best-documented rare earth carbonatite occurrence.
regulatory_notes: Note that the Mindat locality for this name is about 110 km off; the provincial coordinates were used.

name: True North Mine and Mill
description: Formerly San Gold, then Klondex. About 62,000 ha and a fully permitted 1,300 t/day mill. A March 2026 preliminary economic assessment outlines about 58,000 oz/yr over 11 years.
regulatory_notes: The restart uses existing permits; no new Environment Act filing was found. First Nation relationships are not documented in the sources consulted — a gap worth closing.

name: Central Mine (Bissett)
description: Historic gold mine, one of five priority legacy sites.

name: Wanipigow sand quarry
description: More than 41 contiguous quarry leases about 160 km north of Winnipeg. Inferred resource of 24.4 Mt of low-iron glass sand.
regulatory_notes: Licence No. 3285 issued 16 May 2019. A Notice of Alteration reducing volume and footprint produced licence 3285 R, approved July 2023 by the department — no Commission hearing. Hollow Water's chief and council supported the project and signed a participation agreement; the Wilderness Committee says they waived Crown consultation. Some members opposed it through Camp Morningstar, citing sacred sites, and criticised the use of a minor alteration to make a substantial change. The cleanest contrast with Sio Silica anywhere in this catalogue.

name: Selkirk glass manufacturing facility
status: Licensed; solar plans on hold, float-glass pivot
description: A 121-acre site on the CP subdivision using Selkirk's wastewater effluent. Up to $880M estimated. In September 2026 the company was promoting a 600 t/day float-glass plant instead, noting Canada has no domestic float-glass production.
regulatory_notes: Environment Act licence No. 3401 was issued on 3 May 2023, the day after a registry letter (2 May 2023) said a Clean Environment Commission hearing was not recommended, so there was no Commission referral. An earlier version of this note gave 14 February 2024 as the approval date; that is not the licence date. The environment minister went on record in February 2024 explaining how this project differed from Sio Silica, which was refused on 16 February 2024. Technical reviewers had questioned the company's lack of glass-making experience and whether Wanipigow sand could reach solar purity.

name: SiMbA sand extraction (formerly Vivian / CanWhite)
description: Airlift extraction of silica from the Winnipeg Sandstone aquifer, piped as slurry to a separately licensed plant. The original plan was 1.36 Mt/yr over 24 years from more than a thousand wells, up to 7,200 over time. The aquifer supplies drinking water to about 100,000 people.
regulatory_notes: The only mineral project in the Commission's record. Referred in November 2021 for significant public interest. Twelve hearing days, 27 February to 15 March 2023, in Steinbach, Anola and Beausejour. The June 2023 report made eight recommendations and said the Commission could not state with confidence that the effects were understood — it declined to recommend either way. A draft licence was circulated in September 2023. On 16 February 2024 the minister refused it, saying the risk was simply too great; the company called the decision political. Springfield council voted against twice and was overruled by the Municipal Board; a phone-in referendum ran about 95% against. The Métis Federation intervened. Participants received no funding. Re-filed as SiMbA in October 2025 covering years 0–4 only, with an equity offer to Brokenhead Ojibway Nation reportedly worth more than $10M a year — a First Nation the company had not consulted the first time round. No decision found.

name: Vivian Sand processing facility
description: Processing plant fed by the slurry line.
regulatory_notes: Environment Act licence No. 3367 was issued to CanWhite Sands Corp. on 16 December 2021, separately from the extraction project. That split let one half proceed while the other was contested. No Commission referral was found for the processing plant (not confirmed).

name: Port of Churchill
description: The only Arctic deepwater port connected to the North American rail network. regulatory_notes: Port of Churchill Plus was referred to the federal Major Projects Office on 11 September 2025 — rail upgrade, icebreaking, an all-weather road and a new energy corridor. Still pre-development. $175M of federal funding over five years announced March 2025.
